raw: The main purposes of this Act are— (a) to amend the Confiscation Act 1997 in relation to unexplained wealth; and (b) to amend the Control of Weapons Act 1990 in relation to designated areas; and (c) to amend the Crimes Act 1958 to provide that when an application is made for an order directing a person to undergo the taking of a Victoria sample or the conduct of a physical examination, that person may appear at the hearing of the application by audio visual link; and (d) to amend the Crimes (Assumed Identities) Act 2004 in relation to certain authorisations; and (e) to amend the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981— (i) in relation to the destruction or disposal of certain things seized or otherwise acquired by Victoria Police; and (ii) to provide for the display of things seized under a warrant; and (f) to amend the Firearms Act 1996— (i) to prohibit certain possession and distribution of instructions for manufacture of a firearm; and (ii) to provide for the display of things seized under a warrant; and (iii) to make other minor and technical amendments to that Act; and (g) to amend the Criminal Procedure Act 2009— (i) to make amendments related to the amendments referred to in paragraph (f)(i); and (ii) to make other minor and technical amendments to that Act; and (h) to amend the Interpretation of Legislation Act 1984— (i) in relation to prescribing matters by reference in Codes, definitions for all Acts and subordinate instruments and delegations and appointments; and (ii) to provide for the appointment of non-citizens to a public office; and (i) to amend the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004— (i) to provide for targeted information disclosure and to preserve the confidential nature of that information and prohibit its publication; and (ii) in relation to applications by a registrable offender for suspension of reporting obligations; and (iii) to make other miscellaneous amendments to improve the operation of that Act; and (j) to amend the Summary Offences Act 1966— (i) to make it an offence not to comply with a direction, given by a police officer, to remove a face covering worn at a public protest; and (ii) to make it an offence to secure a person to another person, or to a surface or a thing, at a public protest; and (iii) to make it an offence to publicly display symbols of certain terrorist organisations; and (iv) to replace the offence of disturbing religious worship with modernised offences; and (k) to make technical amendments to the Surveillance Devices Act 1999; and (l) to amend the Victoria Police Act 2013— (i) to provide for the transport of certain persons and the exercise of certain functions by police officers in New South Wales and South Australia; and (ii) to provide further functions and powers of protective services officers in relation to transporting, guarding and accompanying certain persons at medical settings and establishing and guarding crime scenes; and (iii) to further provide for disciplinary and probation matters; and (iv) to require the Chief Commissioner to consult with the Minister before issuing a code of conduct.

target_act: Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981
new: Division 5—Destruction in other circumstances Subdivision 1—Preliminary 96A Definitions In this Division— appeal period means, in relation to a conviction, the period ending— (a) if the period provided for an appeal against the conviction has elapsed without the conviction having been appealed, at the end of that period; or (b) if the conviction is appealed, when the appeal is abandoned or finally determined; applicable offence means an offence against section 36B, Part IIIA or Part V; conviction includes a finding of guilt by a court, whether or not a conviction is recorded; destruction direction means a direction given under section 96B(1), 96C(1), 96M or 96N(1); destruction warning has the meaning given by section 96G; illicit thing means— (a) a drug of dependence; or (b) a category 1 precursor chemical; or (c) a category 2 precursor chemical; or (d) an instrument, device or substance that is used, or has been used, or is capable of being used, for or in— (i) the cultivation, manufacture, sale or use of a thing referred to in paragraph (a), (b), or (c); or (ii) preparation for the cultivation, manufacture, sale or use of a thing referred to in paragraph (a), (b) or (c); or (e) a psychoactive substance; or (f) an instrument, device or substance that is used, or has been used, or is capable of being used, for or in— (i) the production, sale or commercial supply of a psychoactive substance; or (ii) preparation for the production, sale or commercial supply of a psychoactive substance; or (g) a Schedule 4 poison; or (h) a Schedule 8 poison; or (i) a Schedule 9 poison; or (j) a category 3 precursor apparatus; independent testing direction means a direction given on an application under section 96L(1); no sample certificate has the meaning given by section 96E(1); thing governed by this Division means a thing that— (a) is— (i) seized by a member of Victoria Police personnel under a warrant or otherwise under any enactment or in the exercise of a power at common law; or (ii) lost or abandoned and then found by, or given to, a member of Victoria Police personnel; and (b) either— (i) is an illicit thing; or (ii) is seized because it is suspected of being an illicit thing. Subdivision 2—Directions to destroy thing governed by this Division 96B Destruction or disposal of thing if offence not to be charged (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may direct in writing that a thing governed by this Division is to be destroyed or disposed of if— (a) the thing is an illicit thing; and (b) at least 3 months have elapsed since the thing was— (i) seized; or (ii) found by or given to a member of Victoria Police personnel; and (c) no offence has been charged in relation to the thing; and (d) the Chief Commissioner of Police— (i) is satisfied that no offence is to be charged in relation to the thing; and (ii) certifies to that effect in the direction; and (e) the Chief Commissioner of Police— (i) is satisfied, in accordance with section 96D, that the thing is not to be returned; and (ii) certifies to that effect in the direction; and (f) the thing is not required under confiscation legislation. (2) A reference in this section to an offence is a reference to an offence against a law of— (a) Victoria; or (b) another State; or (c) a Territory; or (d) the Commonwealth. 96C Destruction or disposal of seized thing after an offence has been charged (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may direct in writing that a thing that is governed by this Division, and in relation to which at least one applicable offence has been charged, is to be destroyed or disposed of if— (a) the thing is an illicit thing; and (b) destruction or disposal of the thing is permitted, in respect of each affected person, by either subsection (3) or (4); and (c) if, under subsection (5), the evidentiary requirements set out in subsection (6) must be met, those requirements have been met; and (d) the Chief Commissioner of Police— (i) is satisfied, in accordance with section 96D, that the thing is not to be returned; and (ii) certifies to that effect in the direction; and (e) the thing is not required under confiscation legislation. (2) A person is an affected person for the purposes of this section if the person is, or was, charged with an applicable offence in relation to the thing in respect of which the direction under subsection (1) is to be issued. (3) Destruction or disposal of the thing is permitted in respect of an affected person if— (a) the person is deceased; or (b) the proceeding on that charge has concluded and— (i) if the person was convicted, the appeal period for that conviction has ended; and (ii) the person is not charged with any other offences (whether against the law of Victoria, another State, a Territory or the Commonwealth) in relation to the thing. (4) Additionally, destruction or disposal of the thing is permitted in respect of an affected person if— (a) a warrant to arrest the person has been issued in relation to the applicable offence but the person has absconded; or (b) the proceeding on that charge has not concluded but— (i) the only offences in relation to the thing with which the person is charged are offences against the law of Victoria; and (ii) the person has been served with a destruction warning in respect of the thing; and (iii) a copy of the destruction warning has been filed with the relevant court as required by section 96K; and (iv) the thing was seized on or after the commencement of this section. (5) The evidentiary requirements set out in subsection (6) must be met if it is under subsection (4) that destruction or disposal is permitted in respect of one or more affected persons. (6) The evidentiary requirements are that— (a) if the thing is a kind of thing from which it is possible to take a sample, either— (i) a sample that is sufficient to be analysed or examined has been taken by an analyst or botanist; or (ii) an analyst or botanist has issued a no sample certificate in respect of the thing; and (b) there is evidence of whichever of the following aspects of the thing that, in the opinion of a member of Victoria Police personnel, are relevant to the offences that relate to the thing (if any)— (i) the appearance and size of the thing; and (ii) if the thing is the kind of thing that has a quantity or amount, that quantity or amount; and (iii) any other physical aspect of the thing; and (c) the Chief Commissioner of Police is satisfied that a member of Victoria Police personnel has arranged for the retention of the evidence referred to in paragraph (b) that is in the custody of Victoria Police. (7) An analyst or botanist who is to take samples of a thing as described in subsection (6)(a)(i) is authorised— (a) to possess the thing for that purpose; and (b) to supply the samples and any remainder of the thing to Victoria Police. 96D When return of a thing is not to occur (1) In order to be satisfied, for the purposes of section 96B(1)(e) or 96C(1)(d), that a thing is not to be returned, the Chief Commissioner of Police must either— (a) be satisfied that— (i) reasonable efforts have been made to identify potential recipients to whom it would be lawful and appropriate, to return the thing; and (ii) no such potential recipient has been identified; or (b) be satisfied that, although the reasonable efforts referred to in paragraph (a)(i) have identified one or more potential recipients to whom it would be lawful and appropriate to return the thing— (i) reasonable efforts have been made to return the thing to each of those potential recipients; and (ii) those efforts have not succeeded. (2) The following persons are potential recipients for the purposes of subsection (1)— (a) if the thing was seized from a person, the person from whom it was seized; (b) the lawful owner of the thing (if any); (c) each person who has an interest that entitles the person to possess the thing. (3) In determining whether it would be lawful to return the thing to a particular person, the fact that this would involve a member of Victoria Police personnel undertaking supply that is prohibited by a provision of this Act or the regulations is to be disregarded. 96E No sample certificate (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may request that an analyst or botanist determine whether or not to issue a certificate (a no sample certificate) to the effect that it is not practicable to— (a) take a sample of a thing governed by this Division in a way that yields a sample that is sufficient to be analysed or examined; and (b) retain that sample. (2) The analyst or botanist must issue the no sample certificate if satisfied that it is not practicable to take and retain the sample as described in subsection (1). (3) Otherwise, the analyst or botanist must refuse to issue the no sample certificate. 96F Effect of destruction direction A destruction direction under section 96B(1) or 96C(1) authorises any member of Victoria Police personnel to destroy or dispose of the thing to which the direction relates. Subdivision 3—Notifications and independent analysis and examination 96G What is a destruction warning? (1) A destruction warning is a notice that— (a) relates to a thing governed by this Division; and (b) explains the circumstances in which the thing may be destroyed or disposed of in accordance with this Division, including, in particular— (i) when the evidentiary requirements set out in section 96C(6) must be met; and (ii) what those evidentiary requirements are; and (c) explains the effect of sections 57 and 58 of the Victoria Police Act 2013 in relation to the thing, including the circumstances (if any) in which the thing may be disposed of under those sections. (2) Additionally, the following information must be included in a destruction warning that is to be served on a person charged with an applicable offence in relation to the thing— (a) an explanation of section 96L; (b) an explanation of the importance of the person on whom it is served obtaining legal representation; (c) advice that the person on whom it is served has the right, if eligible, to legal aid under the Legal Aid Act 1978; (d) details of how to contact Victoria Legal Aid. 96H Destruction warning to be served following seizure (1) This section applies if a thing— (a) is seized under a warrant or otherwise under any enactment or in the exercise of a power at common law; and (b) the thing either— (i) is an illicit thing; or (ii) is seized because it is suspected of being an illicit thing. (2) If the thing is seized from land or premises at which no owner or occupier is present at the time of seizure, a destruction warning relating to the thing must be served on each owner or occupier of the land or premises. (3) If the thing is seized from a vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft the owner of which is not present at the time of seizure, a destruction warning relating to the thing must be served on the owner of the vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft. (4) If, at the time that the thing is seized, the police officer who seizes it considers that a particular person is likely to be charged with an offence in relation to the thing, a destruction warning relating to the thing must be served on that person. (5) A destruction warning that is required to be served by subsection (2), (3) or (4) must be served— (a) by a member of Victoria Police personnel; and (b) as soon as practicable after the thing is seized. 96I Destruction warning to be served following charging of offence If a person is charged with an offence in relation to a thing governed by this Division, and the person has not previously been served with a destruction warning in relation to that thing, a destruction warning relating to that thing must be served on that person— (a) by a member of Victoria Police personnel; and (b) as soon as practicable after the person is charged. 96J Other destruction warnings may be given A member of Victoria Police personnel may serve a destruction warning relating to a thing governed by this Division on— (a) a person whom the member suspects has an interest in the thing; or (b) a person whom the member considers is likely to be charged with an offence in relation to the thing. 96K Filing of destruction warning with relevant court (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police must ensure that if— (a) one or more destruction warnings are, or are required to be, served in relation to a thing; and (b) a person is charged with an applicable offence in relation to that thing— a copy of one of the destruction warnings is filed in the proceeding for that charge. (2) The court must ensure a copy of the destruction warning is made available to each accused in the criminal proceeding at the first hearing in the proceeding. 96L Analysis or examination of samples on application by accused (1) A person who is charged with an offence in relation to a thing governed by this Division may apply to the Chief Commissioner of Police for a direction in writing that provides for the supply of a sample of the thing to an entity that— (a) is eligible under subsection (2); and (b) is nominated in the application— for the purposes of analysing or examining the sample. (2) The following are eligible to receive a sample— (a) an analyst; (b) a botanist; (c) a declared testing facility; (d) an accredited laboratory. (3) If— (a) the Chief Commissioner of Police receives an application under subsection (1); and (b) that application relates to a thing from which no sample has yet been taken as described in section 96C(6)(a)(i); and (c) the Chief Commissioner of Police is not required, by subsection (4), to refuse the application— the Chief Commissioner of Police must request, under section 96E(1), that an analyst or botanist determine whether to issue a no sample certificate for that thing. (4) The Chief Commissioner of Police must refuse an application under subsection (1) if— (a) a no sample certificate has been issued in respect of the thing in respect of which the application is made; or (b) the recipient nominated by the applicant is not eligible under subsection (2); or (c) the entity nominated by the applicant is in a jurisdiction other than Victoria and any of the following things would not permitted by the laws applying in that jurisdiction (even if an independent testing direction were given)— (i) supply, to the recipient, of a sample of the thing in respect of which the application is made; (ii) anything necessary to effect supply of such a sample to the recipient; (iii) possession of such a sample by the recipient; or (d) the thing in respect of which the application is made is a kind of thing from which it is not possible to take a sample. (5) Otherwise, the Chief Commissioner of Police must grant the application. (6) If the Chief Commissioner of Police gives an independent testing direction in respect of a thing of which a sample has not yet been taken, the Chief Commissioner of Police must include in the direction a requirement that a sample of the thing be taken by an analyst or botanist. (7) If an independent testing direction is given, the following things are authorised— (a) the supply— (i) of the sample to which the direction relates; and (ii) by a member of Victoria Police personnel; and (iii) to the entity specified in the direction; (b) if the entity specified in the direction is an analyst or a botanist, possession of the sample by the analyst or botanist for the purposes of analysis or examination; (c) after the sample has been analysed or examined, the return— (i) of the remaining sample (if any); and (ii) by the entity specified in the direction; and (iii) to a member of Victoria Police personnel. Subdivision 4—Destruction or disposal of samples 96M Destruction or disposal of sample if offence not to be charged (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may direct in writing that a sample of a thing governed by this Division, taken under this Part by an analyst or botanist, is to be destroyed or disposed of if— (a) at least 3 months have elapsed since the thing was— (i) seized; or (ii) found by or given to a member of Victoria Police personnel; and (b) no offence has been charged in relation to the thing; and (c) the Chief Commissioner of Police— (i) is satisfied that no offence is to be charged in relation to the thing; and (ii) certifies to that effect in the direction. (2) Nothing in this section limits any other power under this Act. 96N Destruction or disposal of sample after an offence has been charged (1) If— (a) an analyst or botanist takes a sample under this Part of a thing that is governed by this Division; and (b) an applicable offence is charged in relation to that thing; and (c) destruction or disposal of that sample is permitted under subsection (2)— the Chief Commissioner of Police may direct in writing that the sample is to be destroyed or disposed of. (2) Destruction or disposal of the sample is permitted if, for each person charged with an applicable offence referred to in subsection (1)(b)— (a) the person is deceased; or (b) a warrant to arrest the person has been issued in relation to the applicable offence but the person has absconded; or (c) the proceeding on that charge has concluded and— (i) if the person was convicted, the appeal period for that conviction has ended; and (ii) the person is not charged with any other offences (whether against the law of Victoria, another State, a Territory or the Commonwealth) in relation to the thing referred to in subsection (1)(a). (3) Nothing in this section limits any other power under this Act. 96O Effect of destruction direction A destruction direction under section 96M(1) or 96N(1) authorises any member of Victoria Police personnel to destroy or dispose of the sample to which the direction relates. Subdivision 5—Records 96P Record keeping (1) As soon as practicable after a member of Victoria Police personnel destroys or disposes of a thing in accordance with a destruction direction, the member must give the Chief Commissioner of Police a written report setting out— (a) details of the thing that was destroyed or disposed of; and (b) details of the circumstances surrounding the destruction or disposal. (2) The Chief Commissioner of Police must keep a copy of the following— (a) each destruction direction; (b) each no sample certificate; (c) each independent testing direction; (d) a record of the determination of each application made under section 96L(1); (e) each report given under subsection (1). 96Q Request for copy of record (1) The following persons may request in writing a copy of a document that the Chief Commissioner of Police is required to keep under section 96P(2)— (a) if the thing to which the document relates was seized from land or premises, a person who owned or occupied that land or premises when the thing was seized or destroyed or disposed of; (b) if the thing to which the document relates was seized from a vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft— (i) the owner of the vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft; or (ii) a person who, at the time the seizure occurred, owned or occupied the land or premises at which the vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft was located; (c) a person charged with an offence in respect of the thing to which the document relates; (d) the legal representative of a person referred to in paragraph (a), (b) or (c). (2) As soon as practicable after a person makes a request under subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police must cause the person to be provided with a copy of the document. Subdivision 6—Oversight by the IBAC 96R Functions of the IBAC The IBAC has the following functions under this Subdivision— (a) to monitor the giving of destruction directions under section 96C(1) in reliance on section 96C(4)(b); (b) to monitor the refusing of applications for independent testing directions; (c) to make recommendations to the Chief Commissioner of Police, and to report to the Minister for Police and the Chief Commissioner of Police, in relation to its other functions under this Subdivision. 96S IBAC to be given reasonable assistance The Chief Commissioner of Police must give, and must ensure that any other member of Victoria Police personnel gives, the IBAC any assistance that the IBAC reasonably requires to enable the IBAC to perform its functions under this Act. 96T Chief Commissioner of Police must give annual report to IBAC (1) As soon as practicable after the end of a calendar year, the Chief Commissioner of Police must give the IBAC a report under this section in respect of that year. (2) A report under this section in respect of a particular calendar year must set out the following information— (a) the number of destruction directions under section 96C(1) given during that calendar year in reliance on section 96C(4); (b) for each direction referred to in paragraph (a)— (i) the day on which it was given; and (ii) the thing in respect of which it was given; and (iii) the number of persons who were affected persons, within the meaning of section 96C, in relation to the thing in respect of which the direction was given; and (iv) the offences charged in relation to the thing in respect of which the direction was given; and (v) the day on which each destruction warning was served as described in section 96C(4)(b)(ii), if applicable; and (vi) the day on which a copy of a destruction warning was filed as described in section 96C(4)(b)(iii), if applicable; and (vii) whether a sample was taken of the thing in respect of which the direction was given; and (viii) if a no sample certificate was issued as described in section 96C(6)(a)(ii) in relation to the direction, the day the certificate was issued; (c) how many applications for independent testing directions were made during that calendar year; (d) how many applications for independent testing directions were refused during that calendar year; (e) the reasons for each refusal referred to in paragraph (d); (f) if the IBAC has notified the Chief Commissioner of Police under subsection (3) that additional information is required, that information. (3) If the IBAC considers that it would be assisted in the performance of its functions under this Division if additional information were included in a report under this section, the IBAC may give the Chief Commissioner of Police a written notice identifying that information. (4) A written notice under subsection (3)— (a) may identify the additional information either by specifying the information itself or a class of information; and (b) may specify that it applies only in relation to the report in respect of a particular calendar year. 96U IBAC to review certain actions (1) As soon as practicable after the end of each calendar year, the IBAC must conduct a review of the reviewable actions that occurred during that year. (2) The following are reviewable actions for the purposes of this section— (a) the giving of a destruction direction under section 96C(1) in reliance on section 96C(4); (b) the refusing of an application for an independent testing direction. (3) In conducting a review of actions referred to in subsection (2)(a), the IBAC must assess whether the requirements set out in section 96C(4)(b)(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) and (6) were met in respect of the giving of the destruction directions. (4) In conducting a review of actions referred to in subsection (2)(b), the IBAC must assess whether section 96L(4) and (5) were complied with in respect of each refusal of an application for an independent testing direction. (5) The IBAC may decide that a review under subsection (1) in respect of a particular calendar year is to be a review of only a proportion of the reviewable actions that occurred during that year. (6) If the IBAC decides to review only a proportion of the reviewable actions, the IBAC must select the actions to be reviewed, having regard to— (a) the need for the selection to enable a review that appropriately monitors— (i) the exercise of the power to give a destruction direction under section 96C(1) in reliance on section 96C(4); and (ii) the exercise of the power to refuse an application for an independent testing direction; and (b) any other matter the IBAC considers relevant. 96V Powers in relation to reviews (1) Subject to subsection (2), the IBAC may, at any time— (a) enter at any time premises occupied by Victoria Police at which the IBAC reasonably believes there are documents relevant to the IBAC's functions referred to in section 96R(a) and (b); and (b) access, inspect or copy any document found at those premises; and (c) do anything necessary or convenient to be done to enable an inspection to be carried out under this section. (2) The IBAC may do a thing under subsection (1) only after first notifying the Chief Commissioner of Police of the time at which IBAC intends to do that thing. 96W Recommendations to Chief Commissioner of Police The IBAC may at any time make recommendations to the Chief Commissioner of Police about action that should be taken in relation to a matter arising out of a review under section 96U(1). 96X Reports to Minister for Police and Chief Commissioner of Police The IBAC must report the results of a review under section 96U(1) to the Minister for Police and the Chief Commissioner of Police. Subdivision 7—Miscellaneous 96Y Annual reports (1) As soon as practicable after the end of each calendar year, the Chief Commissioner of Police must submit to the Minister for Police a report that includes the following information— (a) how many of the following things were given, issued or provided during that calendar year— (i) destruction directions under section 96B(1); (ii) destruction directions under section 96C(1); (iii) destruction directions under section 96M(1); (iv) destruction directions under section 96N(1); (v) no sample certificates; (vi) independent testing directions; (vii) reports under section 96P(2); (b) how many applications for independent testing directions were refused during that calendar year; (c) any other information that the Minister for Police considers appropriate. (2) The Minister for Police must cause a report under subsection (1) to be laid before each House of the Parliament within 12 sitting days of that House after it is received by the Minister. 96Z Delegation (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may delegate, either generally or in a particular case, a function set out in subsection (2) to— (a) a police officer of or above the rank of Inspector who is specified in the delegation; or (b) each police officer who— (i) is of or above the rank of Inspector; and (ii) belongs to a class specified in the delegation. (2) The functions that may be delegated are the functions of giving a destruction direction under section 96B(1) or 96C(1). (3) A delegation under subsection (1) must be in writing. 96ZA Return of things governed by this Division (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may direct a member of Victoria Police personnel to return a thing governed by this Division to a specified person if satisfied— (a) that the person to whom the thing is to be returned is— (i) if the thing was seized from a person, the person from whom it was seized; or (ii) the lawful owner of the thing (if any); or (iii) a person who has an interest that entitles the person to possess the thing; and (b) returning the thing to that person would be lawful and appropriate. (2) A provision of this Act or the regulations that would prohibit a member of Victoria Police personnel from complying with a direction under subsection (1) does not have that effect. (3) In determining, under subsection (1)(b), whether the return of the thing would be lawful, the Chief Commissioner of Police is to disregard whether this would involve the member of Victoria Police personnel undertaking supply that, but for subsection (2), would be prohibited by a provision of this Act or the regulations.

(2) The Chief Commissioner of Police must keep a copy of the following— (a) each destruction direction; (b) each no sample certificate; (c) each independent testing direction; (d) a record of the determination of each application made under section 96L(1); (e) each report given under subsection (1). 96Q Request for copy of record (1) The following persons may request in writing a copy of a document that the Chief Commissioner of Police is required to keep under section 96P(2)— (a) if the thing to which the document relates was seized from land or premises, a person who owned or occupied that land or premises when the thing was seized or destroyed or disposed of; (b) if the thing to which the document relates was seized from a vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft— (i) the owner of the vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft; or (ii) a person who, at the time the seizure occurred, owned or occupied the land or premises at which the vehicle, boat, vessel or aircraft was located; (c) a person charged with an offence in respect of the thing to which the document relates; (d) the legal representative of a person referred to in paragraph (a), (b) or (c). (2) As soon as practicable after a person makes a request under subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner of Police must cause the person to be provided with a copy of the document. Subdivision 6—Oversight by the IBAC 96R Functions of the IBAC The IBAC has the following functions under this Subdivision— (a) to monitor the giving of destruction directions under section 96C(1) in reliance on section 96C(4)(b); (b) to monitor the refusing of applications for independent testing directions; (c) to make recommendations to the Chief Commissioner of Police, and to report to the Minister for Police and the Chief Commissioner of Police, in relation to its other functions under this Subdivision. 96S IBAC to be given reasonable assistance The Chief Commissioner of Police must give, and must ensure that any other member of Victoria Police personnel gives, the IBAC any assistance that the IBAC reasonably requires to enable the IBAC to perform its functions under this Act. 96T Chief Commissioner of Police must give annual report to IBAC (1) As soon as practicable after the end of a calendar year, the Chief Commissioner of Police must give the IBAC a report under this section in respect of that year. (2) A report under this section in respect of a particular calendar year must set out the following information— (a) the number of destruction directions under section 96C(1) given during that calendar year in reliance on section 96C(4); (b) for each direction referred to in paragraph (a)— (i) the day on which it was given; and (ii) the thing in respect of which it was given; and (iii) the number of persons who were affected persons, within the meaning of section 96C, in relation to the thing in respect of which the direction was given; and (iv) the offences charged in relation to the thing in respect of which the direction was given; and (v) the day on which each destruction warning was served as described in section 96C(4)(b)(ii), if applicable; and (vi) the day on which a copy of a destruction warning was filed as described in section 96C(4)(b)(iii), if applicable; and (vii) whether a sample was taken of the thing in respect of which the direction was given; and (viii) if a no sample certificate was issued as described in section 96C(6)(a)(ii) in relation to the direction, the day the certificate was issued; (c) how many applications for independent testing directions were made during that calendar year; (d) how many applications for independent testing directions were refused during that calendar year; (e) the reasons for each refusal referred to in paragraph (d); (f) if the IBAC has notified the Chief Commissioner of Police under subsection (3) that additional information is required, that information. (3) If the IBAC considers that it would be assisted in the performance of its functions under this Division if additional information were included in a report under this section, the IBAC may give the Chief Commissioner of Police a written notice identifying that information. (4) A written notice under subsection (3)— (a) may identify the additional information either by specifying the information itself or a class of information; and (b) may specify that it applies only in relation to the report in respect of a particular calendar year. 96U IBAC to review certain actions (1) As soon as practicable after the end of each calendar year, the IBAC must conduct a review of the reviewable actions that occurred during that year. (2) The following are reviewable actions for the purposes of this section— (a) the giving of a destruction direction under section 96C(1) in reliance on section 96C(4); (b) the refusing of an application for an independent testing direction. (3) In conducting a review of actions referred to in subsection (2)(a), the IBAC must assess whether the requirements set out in section 96C(4)(b)(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) and (6) were met in respect of the giving of the destruction directions. (4) In conducting a review of actions referred to in subsection (2)(b), the IBAC must assess whether section 96L(4) and (5) were complied with in respect of each refusal of an application for an independent testing direction. (5) The IBAC may decide that a review under subsection (1) in respect of a particular calendar year is to be a review of only a proportion of the reviewable actions that occurred during that year. (6) If the IBAC decides to review only a proportion of the reviewable actions, the IBAC must select the actions to be reviewed, having regard to— (a) the need for the selection to enable a review that appropriately monitors— (i) the exercise of the power to give a destruction direction under section 96C(1) in reliance on section 96C(4); and (ii) the exercise of the power to refuse an application for an independent testing direction; and (b) any other matter the IBAC considers relevant. 96V Powers in relation to reviews (1) Subject to subsection (2), the IBAC may, at any time— (a) enter at any time premises occupied by Victoria Police at which the IBAC reasonably believes there are documents relevant to the IBAC's functions referred to in section 96R(a) and (b); and (b) access, inspect or copy any document found at those premises; and (c) do anything necessary or convenient to be done to enable an inspection to be carried out under this section. (2) The IBAC may do a thing under subsection (1) only after first notifying the Chief Commissioner of Police of the time at which IBAC intends to do that thing. 96W Recommendations to Chief Commissioner of Police The IBAC may at any time make recommendations to the Chief Commissioner of Police about action that should be taken in relation to a matter arising out of a review under section 96U(1). 96X Reports to Minister for Police and Chief Commissioner of Police The IBAC must report the results of a review under section 96U(1) to the Minister for Police and the Chief Commissioner of Police. Subdivision 7—Miscellaneous 96Y Annual reports (1) As soon as practicable after the end of each calendar year, the Chief Commissioner of Police must submit to the Minister for Police a report that includes the following information— (a) how many of the following things were given, issued or provided during that calendar year— (i) destruction directions under section 96B(1); (ii) destruction directions under section 96C(1); (iii) destruction directions under section 96M(1); (iv) destruction directions under section 96N(1); (v) no sample certificates; (vi) independent testing directions; (vii) reports under section 96P(2); (b) how many applications for independent testing directions were refused during that calendar year; (c) any other information that the Minister for Police considers appropriate. (2) The Minister for Police must cause a report under subsection (1) to be laid before each House of the Parliament within 12 sitting days of that House after it is received by the Minister. 96Z Delegation (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may delegate, either generally or in a particular case, a function set out in subsection (2) to— (a) a police officer of or above the rank of Inspector who is specified in the delegation; or (b) each police officer who— (i) is of or above the rank of Inspector; and (ii) belongs to a class specified in the delegation. (2) The functions that may be delegated are the functions of giving a destruction direction under section 96B(1) or 96C(1). (3) A delegation under subsection (1) must be in writing. 96ZA Return of things governed by this Division (1) The Chief Commissioner of Police may direct a member of Victoria Police personnel to return a thing governed by this Division to a specified person if satisfied— (a) that the person to whom the thing is to be returned is— (i) if the thing was seized from a person, the person from whom it was seized; or (ii) the lawful owner of the thing (if any); or (iii) a person who has an interest that entitles the person to possess the thing; and (b) returning the thing to that person would be lawful and appropriate. new: Part 5D—Authorised disclosures of information to affected persons 70X Definitions for this Part In this Part— affected person means any of the following— (a) a victim of a registrable offence committed by a registrable offender; (b) a parent of a person referred to in paragraph (a) who— (i) is a child; or (ii) was a child at the time the offence occurred; affected person's representative means— (a) a person nominated under section 70ZB by an affected person; or (b) in the case of an affected person included in the victims register, a nominee included in the victims register for that person; authorised person means any of the following— (a) an affected person; (b) a person included in the victims register or previously included in the victims register in relation to the registrable offender; (c) a family member of the affected person, including a parent of the affected person; (d) a member of Victoria Police personnel performing a function, exercising a power or discharging a duty under this Act; (e) a police officer, the Director of Public Prosecutions or a person employed in the Office of Public Prosecutions established under the Public Prosecutions Act 1994 if that police officer or person is investigating an offence; (f) a registered medical practitioner in the course of treatment of an affected person or affected person's representative; (g) a person registered as a psychologist under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law in the course of treatment of an affected person or affected person's representative; (h) a lawyer in the course of consulting that lawyer for legal advice; Director of Public Prosecutions means the Director of Public Prosecutions appointed under section 87AB of the Constitution Act 1975; relevant application means any of the following— (a) an application for a sex offender registration order; (b) an application for a registration exemption order; (c) an application under section 39 or 39A for a suspension order; (d) an application under section 44A to revoke a suspension order; (e) an application under Part 5A for approval of a change of name application; (f) an application under section 70R for approval of an acknowledgement of sex application that includes a change of name; relevant event means any of the following— (a) the making of a sex offender registration order under section 11(1), (2) or (9); (b) a suspension order ceasing to have effect by operation of section 44(1) or 44A(2); (c) the reviving of a suspension order under section 44(2); relevant matter means any of the following— (a) a suspension of reporting obligations under section 45A; (b) a cancellation of suspension of reporting obligations under section 45A; suspension order means an order made by a court under section 40 suspending a registrable offender's reporting obligations; victims register has the same meaning as it has in the Corrections Act 1986. 70Y Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose certain information to affected persons (1) Subject to this section and section 70Z, the Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose any information specified in section 70ZA to an affected person if any of the following applies— (a) the disclosure is made for the purposes of performing functions or exercising powers in relation to any relevant application or relevant matter; (b) a relevant application has been made; (c) a relevant event has occurred. (2) If an affected person has nominated a representative, the Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose information under subsection (1) to the representative on behalf of the affected person. (3) If the affected person is a child, the Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose information under subsection (1) to a parent of the child or a representative nominated by a parent instead of the child or a representative nominated by the child after having regard to— (a) the child's capacity to receive the disclosure or nominate a representative; and (b) any preferences for contact expressed by the child and the child's capacity to express those preferences. (4) This section does not apply if— (a) the disclosure relates to a registrable offender who is a person to whom Division 9 of Part 3 applies; or (b) the disclosure of the information would be contrary to an order made by a court. 70Z Disclosure considerations (1) In deciding whether to disclose specified information under section 70Y the Chief Commissioner of Police must have regard to the following— (a) the welfare of the affected person; (b) the affected person's preferences (if any) as to contact; (c) any other matter the Chief Commissioner of Police considers relevant. (2) The Chief Commissioner of Police may also have regard to— (a) the welfare of any other affected person; and (b) the capacity of the affected person to receive a disclosure, nominate a representative or express a preference as to contact; and (c) if the disclosure under section 70Y(1) is made to a parent or representative of a parent instead of a child, the parent's welfare and capacity to receive a disclosure, nominate a representative or express a preference as to contact. 70ZA Specified information (1) For the purposes of section 70Y(1), the following information is specified about a relevant application or relevant matter— (a) the name of the registrable offender; (b) the nature of the relevant application or relevant matter; (c) in the case of a relevant application made to a court, details about how to find information about the date, time and place of the hearing; (d) the decision of the court or the Chief Commissioner of Police (as the case requires) in relation to the relevant application or relevant matter, including— (i) if the relevant application is an application for a sex offender registration order, the reporting period specified in the order; and (ii) if the relevant application or relevant matter relates to a suspension of reporting obligations, the period for which the registrable offender's reporting obligations are suspended; and (iii) if the relevant application is an application for approval of change of name or approval of an acknowledgement of sex, the name registered and date on which it was registered by the Registrar; (e) the date on which the decision was made by the court or the Chief Commissioner of Police. (2) For the purposes of section 70Y(1), the following information is specified in relation to a relevant event— (a) the name of the registrable offender; (b) in the case of the making of a sex offender registration order under section 11(1), (2) or (9)— (i) the date on which the order was made; and (ii) the reporting period specified in the order; (c) in the case of a suspension order that has ceased to have effect— (i) the order that has ceased to have effect; and (ii) the date on which it ceased to have effect; and (iii) the reason that the order ceased to have effect; (d) if the suspension order has been revived by operation of section 44(2)— (i) the order that has been revived; and (ii) the date on which it was revived; and (iii) the reason that the order has been revived. 70ZB Affected person may nominate contact preferences and representative (1) An affected person may notify the Chief Commissioner of Police from time to time of the affected person's preference as to contact for the purposes of receiving a disclosure of information under section 70Y. (2) An affected person may nominate a representative to receive a disclosure under section 70Y on their behalf. (3) A nomination under subsection (2) must be made in the form approved by the Chief Commissioner of Police and include the name and contact details of the person nominated as a representative. 70ZC Secretary may give Chief Commissioner of Police information included in victims register If requested by the Chief Commissioner of Police for the purposes of disclosing information under this Part, the Secretary may— (a) advise the Chief Commissioner of Police— (i) whether an affected person is included in the victims register in respect of a registrable offence committed by the registrable offender; and (ii) if that affected person is included in the victims register, the name of any nominee; and (b) give to the Chief Commissioner of Police the contact details and contact preferences of an affected person included in the victims register and of any nominee included for that affected person in the victims register. 70ZD Record of contact preferences and details The Chief Commissioner of Police must keep a record of— (a) contact details and contact preferences of an affected person notified under section 70ZB or obtained under section 70ZC; and (b) the name, contact details and contact preferences of any affected person's representative notified under section 70ZB or obtained under section 70ZC. 70ZE Obligation to maintain confidentiality of information disclosed—affected person or affected person's representative (1) An affected person or an affected person's representative to whom information is disclosed under section 70Y must maintain the confidential nature of the information. (2) An affected person or affected person's representative does not fail to maintain the confidential nature of the information merely by— (a) in the case of an affected person's representative or a parent of an affected person, disclosing the information to the affected person on whose behalf the disclosure under section 70Y was received; or (b) in any case, disclosing the information to an authorised person. (3) A disclosure in circumstances referred to in subsection (2) does not affect the confidential nature of the information. (4) For the purposes of this section, information disclosed under section 70Y is no longer confidential in nature if it lawfully enters the public domain. 70ZF Obligation to maintain confidentiality— authorised persons and third parties (1) This section applies to a person who— (a) receives information that was disclosed to an affected person or an affected person's representative under section 70Y; and (b) knows or ought reasonably to have known that the information was disclosed to an affected person or an affected person's representative under section 70Y by the Chief Commissioner of Police. (2) The person must maintain the confidential nature of that information. (3) For the purposes of this section, information disclosed under section 70Y is no longer confidential in nature if it lawfully enters the public domain. 70ZG Offence to publish information disclosed under this Part (1) A person must not publish any information about a registrable offender if— (a) the information was disclosed to an affected person or an affected person's representative under section 70Y; and (b) the person knows or ought reasonably to have known that the information was disclosed to an affected person or an affected person's representative under section 70Y. Penalty: 60 penalty units in the case of a natural person; 1200 penalty units in the case of a body corporate. (2) A person must not, for the purposes of publication, solicit or obtain from an affected person or an affected person's representative information that was disclosed to that person under section 70Y. Penalty: 120 penalty units or 1 year imprisonment, in the case of a natural person; 1200 penalty units, in the case of a body corporate. (3) This section does not apply to information about a registrable offender that has lawfully entered the public domain. 70ZH Part does not create rights to information or consultation Nothing in this Part— (a) requires the Chief Commissioner of Police to disclose any specified information to an affected person; or (b) creates any right for an affected person to be consulted by the Chief Commissioner of Police in relation to a relevant application or relevant matter.

new: Division 1C—Public protests Subdivision 1—Preliminary 6B Definition of public protest In this Division— public protest means an event that— (a) occurs at a public place, a non-Government school or a post-secondary education institution; and (b) is held to advance, publicise or promote a political, ideological or industrial cause. Subdivision 2—Face coverings at public protests 6C Objectives of Subdivision The objectives of this Subdivision are— (a) to maintain the fundamental right to engage in peaceful protest; and (b) to protect the ability of persons to exercise that right without fear of violence; and (c) to ensure that police can effectively investigate the commission of alleged offences at public protests, including by identifying the alleged offenders; and (d) to promote public safety and to prevent violence at public protests; and (e) to protect persons from harms that arise from the commission of offences at public protests, under the cover of anonymity, involving conduct that is likely to incite hatred, contempt, revulsion or ridicule. 6D Direction to remove face covering worn at public protest (1) A police officer may direct a person who is wearing a face covering to cease wearing the face covering as soon as reasonably practicable if— (a) the person is at a place where a public protest is occurring; and (b) the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that the person— (i) committed an offence at that place while the public protest was occurring; or (ii) intends to commit an offence at that place while the public protest is occurring. (2) When giving a direction under subsection (1), the police officer may also direct the person to neither resume wearing the face covering, nor wear any other face covering, while at a place where the public protest is occurring. (3) A police officer may also direct a person who is wearing a face covering to cease wearing the face covering as soon as reasonably practicable if— (a) the person— (i) has left a place where a public protest was occurring; or (ii) is at a place where a public protest was occurring but is no longer occurring; and (b) no more than a reasonable amount of time has elapsed since the person left the place or the public protest stopped occurring at that place; and (c) the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that the person committed an offence at that place while the public protest was occurring at that place. (4) Immediately before or after giving a direction under subsection (1), (2) or (3), the police officer must warn the person that it is an offence to fail to comply with the direction without a reasonable excuse. (5) A direction under subsection (1), (2) or (3), and a warning under subsection (4), may be given orally or in writing. (6) A person who— (a) has been given a direction under subsection (1), (2) or (3); and (b) has been given a warning under subsection (4)— must not, without reasonable excuse, fail to comply with the direction. Penalty: 5 penalty units. (7) Without limiting what may be a reasonable excuse for failing to comply with a direction given under this section, it is a reasonable excuse that the face covering is being worn reasonably and in good faith for— (a) a genuine religious or cultural purpose; or (b) a genuine medical purpose. Subdivision 3—Locking or securing persons, surfaces and other things at public protests 6E Objectives of Subdivision The objectives of this Subdivision are— (a) to maintain the fundamental right to engage in peaceful protest; and (b) to protect the ability of persons to exercise that right without risk of injury; and (c) to promote public safety and to prevent injury and serious risks to public safety at public protests. 6F Locking or securing one person to another person or a thing at public protest A person must not, without reasonable excuse, use a thing or a substance to lock or otherwise secure any person (including themselves) to another person, or to a surface or other thing, at a place where a public protest is occurring if— (a) those persons, surfaces or things being locked or otherwise secured together— (i) is likely to cause injury to a person other than one of those who is locked or otherwise secured; or (ii) presents a serious risk to public safety; or (b) unlocking or releasing a person who is locked or secured— (i) is likely to cause injury to a person other than one of those who is locked or otherwise secured; or (ii) presents a serious risk to public safety. Penalty: 120 penalty units or imprisonment for 12 months or both. 6G Seizure of container or other thing (1) A police officer may seize a container of a substance, or another thing, if— (a) the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that a person will imminently commit an offence against section 6F using the substance or the thing; and (b) in the case of a container or other thing that is in a person's possession— (i) the police officer has informed that person that the police officer holds the belief referred to in paragraph (a); and (ii) the police officer has asked the person who possesses the container or other thing to hand it over; and (iii) the police officer has warned the person that the police officer may seize the thing or container and may use reasonable force to do so. (2) A police officer may seize a thing (other than a container of a substance) if— (a) a person is locked or otherwise secured using that thing to another person, or to a surface or other thing; and (b) the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that this is the result of the commission of an offence against section 6F; and (c) the police officer has informed the person who is locked or otherwise secured that the police officer holds the belief referred to in paragraph (b); and (d) the police officer has asked that person to hand the thing over (whether or not this may require breaking, unlocking or otherwise modifying or operating the thing); and (e) the police officer has warned the person that the police officer may seize the thing and may use reasonable force to do so. (3) A police officer may seize a container of a substance if— (a) a person is locked or secured to another person, or to a surface or other thing, using the substance; and (b) the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that this is the result of the commission of an offence against section 6F; and (c) the police officer has informed the person who is locked or otherwise secured that the police officer holds the belief referred to in paragraph (b); and (d) the police officer has asked that person to hand the container over; and (e) the police officer has warned the person that the police officer may seize the container and may use reasonable force to do so. (4) If it is necessary for a police officer to use reasonable force to seize the container or other thing, the police officer may do so. (5) Without limiting subsection (4), when seizing a thing other than a container, if it is necessary to break, unlock or otherwise modify or operate the thing in order to seize it, the police officer may do so. (6) If the person hands the container or other thing over when asked to do so under subsection (1)(b)(ii), (2)(d) or (3)(d), the container or other thing is taken to have been seized under subsection (1), (2) or (3) (as the case requires). (7) Nothing in this section authorises the police officer to search a person or to seize anything that is not fully or partially visible immediately before it is seized. 6H Issue of search warrant by magistrate (1) Section 465 of the Crimes Act 1958 applies to and in respect of an offence against section 6F of this Act as if it were an indictable offence. (2) The other provisions of Subdivision (31) of Division 1 of Part III of the Crimes Act 1958 apply in relation to a warrant issued under section 465 of that Act, as applied by subsection (1), as if an offence against section 6F of this Act were an indictable offence.

new: Division 4D—Public display of symbol of terrorist organisation 41N Objectives of Division The objectives of this Division are— (a) to uphold public safety by creating offences relating to the display of symbols that can encourage persons to engage in violence or vilification; and (b) to protect the rights of persons— (i) to participate in society without fear of violence or vilification; and (ii) to demonstrate their religion or belief; and (iii) to enjoy their culture. 41O Definitions and interpretation In this Division— like process has the same meaning as in section 42(1AA); symbol, in relation to an organisation, has the meaning given by section 41P; terrorist organisation has the same meaning as listed terrorist organisation in Part 5.3 of Chapter 5 of the Criminal Code of the Commonwealth. 41P Symbol of an organisation For the purposes of this Division, a symbol is a symbol of an organisation if it is a symbol that the organisation uses, or members of the organisation use, to identify the organisation. 41Q Public display of terrorist organisation symbol (1) A person must not intentionally display a symbol if— (a) the symbol is a symbol of an organisation; and (b) the person knows that the symbol is a symbol of that organisation; and (c) that organisation is a terrorist organisation; and (d) the display— (i) occurs in a public place, a non-Government school or a post-secondary education institution; or (ii) occurs in sight of a person who is in a public place, a non-Government school or a post-secondary education institution. Penalty: 120 penalty units or imprisonment for 12 months or both. (2) A person does not contravene subsection (1) if the display was engaged in reasonably and in good faith— (a) for a genuine academic, artistic, educational, scientific, cultural or religious purpose; or (b) in making or publishing a fair and accurate report of any event or matter of public interest; or (c) in opposition to the ideology or purposes of a terrorist organisation. (3) A person does not contravene subsection (1) if the symbol is displayed on the person's body by means of tattooing or other like process. (4) A law enforcement officer or a member of an intelligence agency does not contravene subsection (1) if the display occurs in the performance of the officer's or member's duties and is done in good faith. (5) A person does not contravene subsection (1) if the display occurs in the course of official duties connected with the administration of the justice system, including the investigation or prosecution of offences or the giving of evidence in a proceeding in a court or tribunal, and is done in good faith. (6) In a proceeding for an offence against subsection (1), it is not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the person knew that the organisation was a terrorist organisation. 41R Direction to remove terrorist organisation symbol from public display (1) A police officer may direct a person to remove a symbol from display if the police officer believes on reasonable grounds the person is committing an offence against section 41Q(1) by displaying the symbol. (2) A police officer may direct a person to remove from display a symbol if— (a) the person is the owner or occupier of a property on which the symbol is being displayed; and (b) the police officer believes on reasonable grounds an offence is being committed against section 41Q(1) by the display of that symbol. (3) A direction under subsection (1) or (2)— (a) may be given orally or in writing; and (b) must include the period within which it is to be complied with. (4) If a direction cannot be given in person, a police officer may leave the written direction under subsection (1) or (2)— (a) at the property on which the symbol is being displayed; or (b) if the display is in or on a vehicle, by affixing or placing the direction on that vehicle in a conspicuous manner. (5) A person must not, without reasonable excuse, contravene a direction given to the person under subsection (1) or (2). Penalty: 10 penalty units. 41S Seizure of thing bearing a terrorist organisation symbol (1) A police officer may seize a thing that is being displayed if— (a) the display— (i) is occurring in a public place, a non-Government school or a post-secondary education institution; or (ii) is occurring in sight of a person who is in a public place, a non-Government school or a post-secondary education institution; and (b) the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that an offence against section 41Q(1) is being committed by that display; and (c) if the thing is being carried or attended by a person— (i) the police officer has informed that person that the police officer holds the belief referred to in paragraph (b); and (ii) the police officer has asked the person who possesses the thing to hand it over; and (iii) the police officer has warned the person that the police officer may seize the thing and may use reasonable force to do so. (2) If it is necessary for a police officer to use reasonable force to seize the thing, the police officer may do so. (3) If the person hands the thing over when asked to do so under subsection (1)(c)(ii), the thing is taken to have been seized under subsection (1). (4) Nothing in this section authorises the police officer to search a person. 41T Issue of search warrant by magistrate (1) Section 465 of the Crimes Act 1958 applies to and in respect of an offence against section 41Q(1) of this Act as if it were an indictable offence. (2) The other provisions of Subdivision (31) of Division 1 of Part III of the Crimes Act 1958 apply in relation to a warrant issued under section 465 of that Act, as applied by subsection (1), as if an offence against section 41Q(1) of this Act were an indictable offence.

new: Assaulting person attending religious assembly (1) A person must not, without lawful excuse, assault a person— (a) arriving at a place to attend a meeting of persons assembled for religious worship; or (b) attending such a meeting; or (c) leaving such a place during or following such a meeting. Penalty: 15 penalty units or imprisonment for 3 months. (2) A reference in subsection (1) to a person arriving at a place to attend a meeting referred to in that subsection includes a person arriving at that place before the meeting has commenced or before any other persons have assembled. 21B Engaging in conduct to intimidate, menace or harass persons attending religious assembly (1) A person must not, without lawful excuse, engage in conduct that the person intends will intimidate, menace or harass a person— (a) arriving at a place to attend a meeting of persons assembled for religious worship; or (b) attending such a meeting; or (c) leaving such a place during or following such a meeting. Penalty: 15 penalty units or imprisonment for 3 months. (2) In a proceeding for an offence against subsection (1), it is not necessary for the prosecution to prove that a person was intimidated, menaced or harassed. (3) A reference in subsection (1) to a person arriving at a place to attend a meeting referred to in that subsection includes a person arriving at that place before the meeting has commenced or before any other persons have assembled. 21C Engaging in conduct to hinder or obstruct persons attending religious assembly (1) A person must not, without lawful excuse, engage in conduct that the person intends will hinder or obstruct a person from— (a) arriving at a place to attend a meeting of persons assembled for religious worship; or (b) attending such a meeting; or (c) leaving such a place during or following such a meeting. Penalty: 15 penalty units or imprisonment for 3 months. (2) In a proceeding for an offence against subsection (1), it is not necessary for the prosecution to prove that a person was hindered or obstructed from doing a thing referred to in subsection (1)(a), (b) or (c). new: When certain seized things become eligible to be collected, and by whom (1) This section applies in relation to a thing that has been seized under— (a) section 6G or 41S; or (b) a search warrant issued under section 465 of the Crimes Act 1958 as applied by section 6H(1) or 41T(1). (2) The seized thing becomes eligible to be collected, in accordance with section 60C— (a) by or on behalf of an eligible person referred to in subsection (3); and (b) at the applicable time under subsection (4). (3) Each of the following persons is an eligible person— (a) the owner of the seized thing; (b) if the seized thing was in the possession of a person when it was seized— (i) the person to whom a police officer gave information under section 6G(1)(b), (2)(c) or (3)(c); or (ii) the person whom a police officer dealt with under section 41S(1)(c)— as the case requires. (4) The applicable time is— (a) when 3 months elapse without a person being charged with an offence against section 6F, 41Q(1) or 41R(5) in respect of the seized thing; or (b) when a decision is made, within the period referred to in paragraph (a), not to charge an offence referred to in that paragraph; or (c) if a person is charged with an offence referred to in paragraph (a), when the proceeding for that offence has concluded without the thing being forfeited under section 60E. 60C Collection of seized thing from police station (1) This section applies in relation to a seized thing that, at an applicable time referred to in section 60B(4), becomes eligible for collection by an eligible person referred to in section 60B(3). (2) The police officer in charge of the police station at which the seized thing is kept must give notice under this section to each person whose status as an eligible person can be discerned from the records of Victoria Police. (3) Notice under this section must— (a) be in writing; and (b) inform the person to whom it is given— (i) that the person has a right to collect the seized thing; and (ii) that the thing will be forfeited to the Crown if not collected. (4) Notice under this section must be given as soon as practicable after the police officer referred to in subsection (2) identifies the person as an eligible person. (5) The police officer in charge of the police station at which the seized thing is kept must allow an eligible person to either— (a) attend that police station and collect the thing; or (b) have another person attend and collect the thing on the eligible person's behalf. 60D Forfeiture of seized thing that is not collected (1) If a seized thing that becomes eligible, under section 60B, for collection under section 60C is not collected before the time specified in subsection (2), the thing is forfeited to the Crown at that time. (2) The time at which the seized thing is forfeited is— (a) if at least one eligible person is given notice under section 60C, 3 months after the last eligible person received that notice; or (b) if no eligible person was given notice under section 60C, 4 months after the time at which the seized thing became eligible, under section 60B, for collection under section 60C. (3) Subject to subsection (4), the Minister may direct that a thing forfeited to the Crown under subsection (1) is to be disposed of in any manner the Minister thinks fit. (4) If a thing is sold under subsection (3), the proceeds of the sale must be paid into the Consolidated Fund. 60E Forfeiture of seized thing in other circumstances (1) This section applies in relation to a thing that has been seized under— (a) section 6G or 41S; or (b) a search warrant issued under section 465 of the Crimes Act 1958 as applied by section 6H(1) or 41T(1); or (c) a power at common law as it applies in relation to an offence against section 6F, 41Q(1) or 41R(5). (2) If a court finds a person guilty, or not guilty by reason of mental impairment, of an offence against section 6F, 41Q(1) or 41R(5) in respect of the seized thing, the seized thing is forfeited to the Crown unless the court orders otherwise. (3) Subject to subsections (4) and (5), the Minister may direct that a thing forfeited to the Crown under subsection (2) is to be disposed of in any manner the Minister thinks fit. (4) The Minister must not dispose of a thing under subsection (3) unless— (a) an appeal in relation to the offence has been abandoned or finally determined; or (b) the period in which such an appeal may be commenced has elapsed without an appeal having been commenced. (5) If a thing is sold under subsection (3), the proceeds of the sale must be paid into the Consolidated Fund.

new: Division 3A—Transport of persons in transit states 59D Object of Division The object of this Division is to enable police officers to transport persons and exercise certain functions in a transit state. 59E Application of Division (1) If anything in this Division is inconsistent with an Act or law of a transit state in relation to the transport of persons in the transit state, the law of the transit state prevails to the extent of the inconsistency. (2) Without limiting subsection (1), this Division does not limit the exercise of any function by a police officer under— (a) this Act (other than this Division) or any other Act or law; or (b) a law of another State or a Territory or the Commonwealth. (3) Nothing in this Division applies to a police officer exercising a function— (a) as a recognised law enforcement officer within the meaning of section 3 of the Police Act 1990 of New South Wales; or (b) as a special constable within the meaning of section 3 of the Police Act 1998 of South Australia; or (c) under any appointment, authorisation or recognition in a transit state; or (d) in a prescribed capacity. 59F When is a person in police custody, care or control? (1) In this Division, a reference to police custody, care or control is a reference to the custody, care or control (as the case may be) of— (a) a person who is in the legal custody of the Chief Commissioner under an Act; or (b) a person who is in custody under the Crimes Act 1958; or (c) a person who is in the care and control of a police officer under— (i) the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022; or (ii) the Youth Justice Act 2024; or (d) a child who is under the care of a police officer under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005; or (e) a person who has been apprehended by a police officer under— (i) the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act 1997; or (ii) the Disability Act 2006; or (f) a person who is otherwise in— (i) the physical or legal custody; or (ii) the care or control— of a police officer under an Act or a law; or (g) a person in prescribed circumstances (if any). (2) For the purposes of this Division, if a person who is in police custody, care or control is transported by a police officer under section 59G, the police custody, care or control of the person does not cease merely because the person is in a transit state. 59G Transport of persons in transit state (1) A police officer may transport a person in a transit state for a reason specified in subsection (2) if the transport of the person, whether by that police officer or another police officer, began in Victoria. (2) For the purposes of subsection (1), the specified reasons are the following— (a) to transit through the transit state to a destination in Victoria, if the police officer transporting the person considers that transiting through the transit state provides a safer or more direct route to the destination than other routes; (b) to obtain medical care for the person, if the police officer transporting the person considers that— (i) the person requires the medical care; and (ii) it is necessary or convenient to obtain the medical care in the transit state; (c) to exercise any of the following functions of the police officer— (i) a function under Part 5.2 or 5.3 of the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022; (ii) in the case of a police officer who is a protective intervener within the meaning of section 3(1) of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005, to place a person referred to in paragraph (b) of the definition of child in section 3(1) of that Act into emergency care in a transit state in accordance with that Act; (iii) if the person is a child aged 10 or 11, to place the person into the care of— (A) a suitable person under section 69(1) of the Youth Justice Act 2024 in a transit state; or (B) if the person is unable to be placed into the care of a suitable person, an appropriate health or welfare agency under section 69(3) of that Act in a transit state; (iv) if the person is subject to a non- custodial supervision order under the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act 1997 and has been apprehended by a police officer in Victoria, to take the person to an appropriate place within the meaning of that Act in a transit state; (v) any other prescribed function; (d) to return the person to Victoria from the transit state if an action or function referred to in paragraph (b) or (c)— (i) has been completed or exercised; or (ii) is unable to be continued or completed. (3) Without limiting subsection (1), the transport of a person under that subsection is taken to begin in Victoria and continue without suspension or interruption, if the physical transport is suspended or interrupted— (a) because the person is receiving medical care; or (b) by the transfer by one police officer of the custody, care or control of the person to another police officer; or (c) for any other reason, provided the person remains in police custody, care or control during that suspension or interruption; or (d) in the prescribed circumstances (if any). (4) If a person is being transported under subsection (1), a police officer may exercise a function referred to in subsection (2)(b) or (c) in relation to that person. (5) For the purposes of this section, any function, obligation, responsibility and immunity under any Act or the common law which apply to a police officer on duty in Victoria apply to a police officer— (a) who is— (i) transporting a person under subsection (1); or (ii) exercising a function under subsection (2)(b) or (c); or (b) who is directing, supervising, accompanying or otherwise assisting another police officer who is— (i) transporting a person under subsection (1); or (ii) exercising a function under subsection (2)(b) or (c). (6) In subsection (5), a reference to any Act includes (but is not limited to) the following— (a) the Victoria Police Act 2013; (b) the Crimes Act 1958; (c) the Youth Justice Act 2024; (d) the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022; (e) the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act 1997; (f) the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005; (g) the Disability Act 2006; (h) the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006; (i) any other prescribed Act. (7) This section does not apply in the prescribed circumstances.
